primer.text: From Explaining Rates you already know why hotter, denser crowds of particles react faster. This note introduces the helper that speeds reactions without being consumed, the catalyst, and the alternative pathway that explains its power. Industrial chemistry leans on these substances every day.

lessons.title: What a catalyst is and is not
sourceHeadings: The effect of a catalyst on rate of reaction
lessons.opening: A catalyst is chemistry's helper that is not used up: it speeds the reaction and walks away unchanged. This lesson pins down the definition, the small amounts needed and the way catalysts appear above reaction arrows.
keyPoints: A catalyst raises the rate of a reaction yet finishes it chemically unchanged.
Catalysts speed up reactions without themselves being altered or consumed.
Only small amounts of a catalyst are normally needed to have an effect.
Weigh a catalyst before and after a reaction and its mass reads exactly the same.
Catalysts are written above or below the reaction arrow rather than in the equation.

low.restatement: A catalyst makes a reaction faster but comes out of the reaction exactly as it went in, so a tiny pinch can serve again and again. Its name is never listed with the reactants, only over the arrow.
low.analogy: It is like a matchmaker at a wedding: the pairing happens faster, but the matchmaker leaves exactly as they arrived.
low.examPointer: Quote both halves of the definition: faster rate and chemically unchanged at the end.

medium.restatement: Catalysts raise the rate of a reaction while remaining chemically unchanged, so their mass is identical before and after. Small amounts suffice, and the catalyst is shown above the reaction arrow because it is not a reactant or product.
medium.analogy: A catalyst behaves like a revolving door: crowds pass through much faster, yet the door itself neither joins the crowd nor wears out.
medium.examPointer: Mention the unchanged mass and the arrow notation when justifying why a catalyst is not in the equation.

check.stem: Which statement is the full definition of a catalyst?

options.text: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction but is chemically unchanged at the end
options.explanation: Both the speed-up and the unchanged state are required.

options.text: A substance that makes reactions happen that would never occur
options.explanation: Catalysts change pace, not possibility.

options.text: A substance consumed to provide energy for the reaction
options.explanation: Catalysts are not consumed and do not fuel reactions.

options.text: Any substance present in small amounts
options.explanation: Small amount is a feature, not the definition.

check.stem: Why do small amounts of catalyst suffice?

options.text: Because the catalyst is not consumed and can keep working
options.explanation: Being unchanged at the end means one batch can process far more reactant.

options.text: Because catalysts are too expensive to waste
options.explanation: Cost may be true industrially, but the chemical reason is non-consumption.

options.text: Because a small mass reacts completely
options.explanation: The catalyst does not react away at all.

options.text: Because catalysts dissolve into the products
options.explanation: Dissolving is not part of catalysis here.

check.stem: Where does the catalyst appear in a chemical equation?

options.text: Above or below the reaction arrow
options.explanation: The arrow position shows the catalyst aids the change without being a reactant.

options.text: On the left with the reactants
options.explanation: That would list it as a reactant, which it is not.

options.text: On the right with the products
options.explanation: It is not produced by the reaction.

options.text: Nowhere, since catalysts are secret
options.explanation: Industrial equations routinely show catalysts over the arrow.

check.stem: A reaction finishes with 2 g of solid catalyst recovered from 2 g added. What does this show?

options.text: The substance acted as a catalyst, unchanged in mass by the reaction
options.explanation: Matching start and end masses are the expected behaviour of a catalyst.

options.text: The catalyst must have doubled in activity
options.explanation: Mass recovery says nothing about activity doubling.

options.text: The catalyst was the product
options.explanation: Products are made by the reaction; the catalyst was present at the start.

options.text: The reaction never happened
options.explanation: The reaction can proceed fully while the catalyst stays unchanged.

check.stem: Which is a consequence of using a catalyst in an industrial process?

options.text: A faster production rate without the catalyst being consumed
options.explanation: Speed rises while the catalyst batch keeps working, which is why industry invests in it.

options.text: The products become different chemicals
options.explanation: Catalysts change the pace, not the identity of the products.

options.text: The equation must be rebalanced
options.explanation: Balancing is untouched by catalysis.

options.text: The reaction becomes irreversible
options.explanation: Reversibility is unaffected by adding a catalyst.

lessons.title: How catalysts work and where industry uses them
sourceHeadings: The effect of a catalyst on rate of reaction
lessons.opening: The shortcut is the secret: a catalyst offers the reaction an alternative pathway with a lower energy hurdle. This lesson walks that mechanism and meets the industrial catalysts built on it.
keyPoints: A catalyst opens a lower-energy route that lets more collisions succeed.
Different processes need different catalysts, but all work on the same principle.
Catalysts attract reactant molecules onto their surface, providing a lower-energy route.
Catalysis raises production rates and reduces energy costs in commercial chemistry.
Enzymes act as catalysts in biological systems.

low.restatement: Instead of the steep hill the reaction normally climbs, a catalyst opens a gentler path, so more particles can make the journey. The same idea serves every industry, and living cells use it too through enzymes.
low.analogy: It is like a mountain road tunnelling through the pass: the summit stays the same, but far more lorries can make the crossing.
low.examPointer: Use the phrase alternative pathway with lower activation energy when explaining how catalysts work.

medium.restatement: A catalyst opens an easier route whose lower energy hurdle lets a greater proportion of collisions succeed, so the rate rises. Atoms on the catalyst surface attract reactant molecules, and the same principle spans industrial processes and the enzymes of living systems.
medium.analogy: A ferry turns a long drive around the bay into a short crossing; the destination is unchanged, but the journey is easier and far more traffic completes it.
medium.examPointer: Link the lowered barrier to more successful collisions, then name surface action and enzymes as extensions.

check.stem: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?

options.text: By providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy
options.explanation: The lower hurdle lets more collisions lead to products.

options.text: By heating the reaction mixture
options.explanation: Catalysts are not heaters; temperature is a separate factor.

options.text: By increasing the concentration of reactants
options.explanation: Concentration is untouched by the catalyst.

options.text: By weakening the products so they form sooner
options.explanation: Product strength is not the mechanism.

check.stem: What happens to the activation energy of the uncatalysed route when a catalyst is added?

options.text: It stays the same; the catalyst opens a new, lower route alongside it
options.explanation: The original pathway still exists; the alternative is simply easier.

options.text: It falls, because the catalyst lowers every barrier
options.explanation: The uncatalysed route is untouched; only the new route is lower.

options.text: It doubles, because two routes now compete
options.explanation: Competition between routes does not raise any barrier.

options.text: It disappears entirely
options.explanation: The catalysed route still has its own, smaller barrier.

check.stem: Iron in the ammonia process and vanadium(V) oxide in the sulfur process are examples of what?

options.text: Different catalysts chosen for different industrial processes
options.explanation: Each process pairs with a catalyst suited to it, all working on the same principle.

options.text: Reactants consumed by their reactions
options.explanation: Both substances are recovered unchanged after the process.

options.text: Products of their reactions
options.explanation: Neither is a product; both pre-date the reaction.

options.text: Fuels burned to heat the processes
options.explanation: They are not burned; they host the reaction on their surfaces.

check.stem: Why does a lower-energy pathway raise the reaction rate?

options.text: A greater proportion of collisions now carry enough energy to react
options.explanation: Lowering the hurdle promotes more ordinary collisions into successful ones.

options.text: Because particles collide less often but harder
options.explanation: Frequency does not fall; the success rate rises.

options.text: Because the catalyst collides with the particles
options.explanation: Collisions with the catalyst surface are part of the route, not the rate logic.

options.text: Because the products leave faster
options.explanation: Product departure is not the rate-determining idea here.

check.stem: Which biological molecules act as catalysts?

options.text: Enzymes
options.explanation: Enzymes catalyse the reactions of living systems on the same lower-pathway principle.

options.text: Fats
options.explanation: Fats store energy; they do not catalyse.

options.text: Sugars
options.explanation: Sugars are respiratory fuels, not catalysts.

options.text: Water molecules
options.explanation: Water is a solvent or reactant here, not the biological catalyst.

glossary.definition: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction but is chemically unchanged at the end.
The minimum energy particles need for a reaction to occur; catalysts open a lower pathway.
The easier reaction route that a catalyst provides, with a lower energy barrier.
A biological molecule that acts as a catalyst in living systems.
A block of metals widely used as catalysts because they donate and accept electrons readily.

workedExample.prompt: a) State the full definition of a catalyst. b) Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction. c) 2.00 g of manganese(IV) oxide is added to hydrogen peroxide solution; at the end the solid is filtered off, dried and re-weighed. State its expected mass and what this shows.
steps: a) A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a reaction but is chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction.
b) It provides an alternative pathway for the reaction with a lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions succeed and the rate rises.

c) The mass reads 2.00 g again: a catalyst's mass is identical before and after, showing it is not consumed — small amounts suffice, and it is written above the reaction arrow rather than in the equation.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Speeds up the reaction, chemically unchanged at the end. b) Alternative pathway with lower activation energy. c) 2.00 g — unchanged, so not consumed.
